passages.t: In the cistern, and Ebed-melech's rescue
passages.happening:
Four officials, Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal and Pashhur, hear Jeremiah telling the people that whoever stays in the city will die by sword, famine and plague, but whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live (verses 1 and 2), and that the city will surely be taken (verse 3). They tell the king that this man must die, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers and of all the people; he is not seeking their welfare but their harm (verse 4). Zedekiah answers that he is in their hands, since the king can do nothing against them (verse 5).

‘So they took Jeremiah and dropped him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king’s son’ (verse 6), in the courtyard of the guard. They let him down with ropes. There was no water in it, only mud, and Jeremiah sank into the mud (verse 6).

Ebed-melech the Cushite, an official in the palace, hears of it (verse 7). He goes to the king, who is sitting at the Benjamin Gate, and tells him these men have done wrong; Jeremiah will starve in the cistern, for there is no more bread in the city (verses 8 and 9). The king tells him to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah out before he dies (verse 10). Ebed-melech takes old rags and worn-out clothes from a storeroom and lets them down by ropes, telling Jeremiah to put them under his arms to pad the ropes (verses 11 and 12). They pull him up, and Jeremiah stays in the courtyard of the guard (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The siege lasted from about January 588 BC to the summer of 587 or 586 BC, and by now famine was severe. Two of the officials appear earlier: Pashhur son of Malchijah had been sent to Jeremiah by the king (21:1), and Jucal was one of the king's envoys (37:3).

Their charge, weakening the hands of the soldiers, is a Hebrew way of saying destroying morale. One of the Lachish letters from these same months uses a very similar phrase, complaining that words from officials in Jerusalem were weakening the people's hands. It does not name Jeremiah, but it shows defeatist talk was a live fear.

Cisterns were cut into rock to hold rainwater. In a long siege this one had run dry, leaving deep mud. To leave a man there was to let him die slowly without shedding his blood.

Ebed-melech, whose name means servant of the king, was a Cushite, a man from Cush, the land south of Egypt on the upper Nile. A foreigner in the palace did what Judah's own leaders would not. His rags under the arms are a small, careful kindness.
passages.later: God later promises Ebed-melech, ‘Because you have trusted in Me, you will escape with your life’ (Jeremiah 39:18). A psalm gives thanks for the same kind of rescue: ‘He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay’ (Psalm 40:2).
passages.hard:
Was Jeremiah guilty of treason, telling soldiers and citizens to surrender to the enemy during a war?

From the officials' point of view the charge was reasonable, and many modern readers feel its force: no city under siege tolerates a public voice urging people to go over to the enemy. Jeremiah's defenders make three points. He did not act for Babylon's sake but spoke what he understood as God's verdict on Judah's broken covenant; his loyalty was to God, not to either empire. Zedekiah himself had sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar in God's name (2 Chronicles 36:13; Ezekiel 17:13-19), so the rebellion was itself a broken oath. And Jeremiah's counsel aimed at saving lives, and the city's fall proved him right.

Readers still differ on how far his stance can serve as a model for dissent today. It rested on a word from God about one moment, and these notes draw no line from it to any nation or war of the present day.
passages.asks: Ebed-melech, an outsider, spoke up when no one else would and was gentle in the rescue. Ask whom you could speak up for this week. And ask what small kindness, like rags to pad the ropes, could make someone's rescue less painful.

passages.t: A last offer to the king
passages.happening:
Zedekiah sends for Jeremiah and meets him at the third entrance of the LORD's house. He wants to ask him something and tells him to hide nothing (verse 14). Jeremiah answers that if he speaks, the king will kill him, and if he gives advice, the king will not listen (verse 15). Zedekiah swears secretly by the LORD that he will not kill him or hand him over (verse 16).

Jeremiah tells him the LORD's word. If the king surrenders to the officers of the king of Babylon, his life will be spared, the city will not be burned, and his household will live (verse 17). If he does not, the city will be handed to the Chaldeans and burned, and he will not escape (verse 18).

Zedekiah says he is afraid of the Judeans who have already deserted to the Chaldeans, that he will be handed over to them and mistreated (verse 19). Jeremiah says they will not hand him over. He pleads with him to obey the LORD's voice, so it will go well with him (verse 20). If he refuses, the women left in the palace will be led out to Babylon's officers, mocking him for trusting friends who misled him; his wives and children will be taken, and the city burned (verses 22 and 23).

Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to let no one know of their talk (verse 24). If the officials ask, he is to say he was pleading not to be sent back to Jonathan's house (verses 25 and 26). The officials do ask, and Jeremiah answers as the king told him (verse 27). He stays in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem is taken (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
This is the last of Zedekiah's secret meetings with Jeremiah. The king knew the truth. He was afraid of his own officials, who had just thrown Jeremiah in a cistern, and afraid of the Judeans who had already gone over to Babylon. Fear of people kept him from obeying God.

The offer was real: surrender, and the city will not burn. Zedekiah could not bring himself to take it.

Jeremiah's answer to the officials in verse 27 kept the king's confidence without telling a lie; he had indeed asked not to be sent back to Jonathan's house in chapter 37.
passages.later: Proverbs names Zedekiah's trap: ‘The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high’ (Proverbs 29:25). Chronicles says Zedekiah ‘stiffened his neck and hardened his heart’ (2 Chronicles 36:13).
passages.asks: Zedekiah knew what God said and was too afraid of people to do it. Ask whose opinion keeps you from obeying God. And ask what a choice made out of fear has already cost you.
